items.title: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe by an estimated 5 °C
items.claim: How much does ocean circulation warm western Europe?

options.text: Not at all — climate is determined by latitude alone

Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) and modelling studies suggest the wider North Atlantic circulation system contributes around 5-10 °C of additional warmth to western Europe
By 30 °C — without it Europe would be like Antarctica

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it broadens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the heat onshore.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that atmospheric heat transport and the southwesterly stationary wave (set up by the Rocky Mountains) are at least as important as ocean heat in distinguishing western from eastern continental winters. The single-cause 'Gulf Stream warms Britain' story is too simple.

The AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021). A collapse would cool Europe and warm the tropics.
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems acting together. The Gulf Stream story is partly true and partly simplified; a teaching answer needs both the ocean and the atmosphere.

items.title: Most rainforest soils are highly weathered and nutrient-poor
items.claim: What surprises about tropical rainforest soil?

options.text: They are deep and extremely fertile

Heavy rainfall leaches soluble nutrients, leaving iron- and aluminium-rich oxisols (latosols); fertility is held in the biomass and recycled rapidly through litter — slash-and-burn agriculture works for only 2-3 years before fertility crashes
They are pure sand with no organic matter

items.reveal_title: Fertility in the trees, not the ground
items.reveal:
High rainfall and temperatures leach soluble nutrients (calcium, potassium, phosphorus) out of the upper soil, leaving heavily weathered, iron-rich red soils. Decomposition is rapid; mycorrhizal networks and shallow root mats intercept nutrients immediately.

Amazonian 'terra preta' (black earth) soils are a notable exception — anthropogenic soils created by pre-Columbian populations using charcoal, bone and food waste, retaining fertility for centuries. They are now studied as a biochar model.

When forest is cleared, the burn temporarily releases biomass nutrients; crops grow for 2-3 years before yields collapse.
items.why: Lush vegetation does not imply fertile soil. The 'rainforest = rich land' assumption has driven destructive agricultural expansion for centuries — and explains why cleared land degrades quickly.

items.title: Choropleth maps show areal data; isoline maps show continuous data
items.claim: What is the difference between choropleth and isoline maps?

options.text: There is no difference — alternative names for the same thing
Choropleth: defined areas (countries, counties) shaded by category. Isoline: lines connecting points of equal value (contours, isobars, isotherms, isohyets)
Isoline maps cannot show climate data

items.reveal:
Choropleth maps assume uniform values within each area; they are vulnerable to the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) — different boundary choices produce different patterns.

Isoline maps (also called isarithmic) treat the variable as a continuous surface. Examples: contour lines (relief), isobars (atmospheric pressure), isotherms (temperature), isohyets (rainfall).

Other techniques: dot maps (each dot represents a count), proportional symbols (size scaled to value), flow lines (volume of movement), cartograms (areas distorted by value).
items.why: Map technique matters. The same data, mapped differently, tells different stories — and the right technique depends on whether the underlying variable is areal or continuous.
